## A simple relationship

Many scientific relationships can first be explored with a small model. The
illustration below shows the three parts of the workflow used in this lesson.

![Observe a system, express a model, and interpret its result.](../assets/model-workflow.svg){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

Suppose a measured response is proportional to an input:

$$
y = kx.
$$

The optional supporting package can keep reusable calculations in one tested
place while the course page concentrates on interpretation.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-example-values
#| tbl-cap: "Responses predicted by a proportional model."
from playground.utils.example import proportional_response

inputs = [0, 1, 2, 3]
[(value, proportional_response(value, rate=2.5)) for value in inputs]
```

## Exercise

::: {teaching="exercise"}
Predict the response for an input of 4 when $k=2.5$. Explain what the value of
$k$ means in this model.
:::

```{python}
#| teaching: exercise
#| eval: false
# Replace the missing value, then run the cell.
proportional_response(4, rate=...)
```

::: {.callout-solution title="Worked solution"}
Substitution gives $y=2.5\times4=10$. The rate $k$ means that the response
increases by 2.5 units for every one-unit increase in the input.
:::

```{python}
#| teaching: solution
proportional_response(4, rate=2.5)
```

## Takeaway

A useful computational example should support the scientific idea rather than
hide it. Put reusable mechanics in a helper only when that makes the authored
lesson clearer.
